generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, approaching an exam is one thing you do, not three. You ask what the exam is for, find out its type and what it asks, and build a revision plan that matches. Done together, in any subject, these turn an exam from a thing to dread into a thing you can prepare for.
generatedProse.worked-example: Two students face the same exam. One revises the way he always does, rereading his notes late into the night, without asking what the exam is for or what type it is. The other brings the three strands together. She sees the exam as a chance to learn, finds out it is an essay exam, and plans two weeks of revision around her weaker topics. Her preparation is stronger, because approaching the exam became one practice rather than three separate things.
generatedProse.summary: Approaching an exam works best when the three strands act as one. You ask what the exam is for, match your preparation to its type, and plan revision around your time and your gaps. It is the whole approach, not any single part, that turns an exam into something you can prepare for.

check.body: A student finds out her exam is an essay exam, treats it as a chance to build her thinking, and plans two weeks of revision around her weaker topics. What does this show?

items.text: Their next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following essay improved.
Nothing; feedback comes at the end, so it cannot affect anything that follows.
Only the mark on the first essay, which cannot now change.
The deadline for the next essay.

feedback.correct: That's right. Using feedback to plan the next piece of work feeds it straight back into your learning, closing the loop and starting the next round stronger. That is the cycle working as it should.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the student did with the feedback, and what improved as a result.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Acting on feedback feeds your next round of learning and preparation, which is why the following essay was stronger. The mark on the first essay cannot change, but the feedback still shapes what comes next.

_items.text: The whole approach at work: she used the purpose and the type to decide what to revise, then planned her time to match.
_items.feedback: Yes. Purpose, type and strategy are all there, working together.

_items.text: Only cramming, because she revised for two weeks.
_items.feedback: Spreading revision over two weeks is a strategy, not cramming.

_items.text: Only the exam type, because she found out it was an essay exam.
_items.feedback: She did more than name the type. She also planned revision to match it.

_items.text: Nothing useful, because the mark is all that counts.
_items.feedback: The mark is not the point here. Her approach is what the scenario shows.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; name the cast directly in the prose (the pack supplies the whole body). The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
